Yeah, that was some really wonderful points by my co-panelists. I think many of us here today are aware of the large-scale inequities within our communities and especially within our cities. Youth contribute innovation solutions to tackling challenges and are key drivers of change, especially as the global urban population is projected to reach 70% by 2050. Thank you for the question, Terry. According to the United Nations, by 2100, the global population is going to reach 11 billion people, and that's 3 billion more than what we see today. And in order to meet this extraordinary growth, we will roughly need about 2.4 trillion square meters of housing and infrastructure. And let me just put this into perspective for people here. This is equivalent to building the area of one Manhattan every month for the next 40 years. So this is the challenge we have in front of us. And having worked with national and local governments in more than 5+ countries, I think the real question is, will our cities just become places where housing is treated as a commodity, where it's bought, sold, and speculated on, or will it even recognize housing as a fundamental right of all young people? Because today young people are pushed out of cities, facing high rents, shrinking pathways to ownership, and also navigating systems that were never designed for them. So what are some of the housing models that can really support youth to continue living in cities and owning home in cities? I think the first is community land trusts, because this offers a powerful model for long-term affordability by placing land under collective stewardship and removing speculative markets, this ensures that housing is accessible across all generations. The second is pioneering cooperative housing. This really provides an alternative system to purely profit-driven systems. So as people have shared ownership, they share responsibility, they share decision-making, and also a sense of belonging. The third is how do we redefine space, right? Microhousing offers a very great pathway for young people, especially in cities like New York. And when these housing are designed well, they can really improve quality of life. And I would just end by saying that these are not just ideas, but these are scalable, adaptable, and already in motion. So only thing it requires is cities willing to experiment, the investment not just in capital, but in young innovators and young leaders. Thank you.

Recognizing that youth play a leading role in implementing and accelerating SDG 11, let us hear from our panelists on how they are contributing and what is needed to scale up these efforts. We will hear from Shreya, Rahman, Alison, and Shushmita. in that order. Shreya?

Amazing. So I'm going to take the question specifically trying to focus on how we can create scalable urban governance models everywhere. So, in order to make that a reality, there are 4 strategies that I would encourage decision-makers to employ over the lifecycle of any project or initiative. Firstly, I would start with visioning. What is the big picture? What are the goals that we're trying to push towards? Those are the starting questions that youth should be involved in answering. Very often, young people are consulted after several rounds of decision-making have already been undergone, And that prevents young people from bringing in new ideas and insights that might help shape the scope of a project or an initiative. Secondly, capacity building for youth. How do we know that young people feel ready and feel like they understand the system that they've been called to comment on? Are youth aware of existing policies and norms? Are they aware of funding or timeline constraints? Doing this capacity building is essential to getting high-quality and actionable feedback, and it also lowers the barrier to entry for minority or under— other under-resourced groups who might not have the policy knowledge or understand the jargon that is often so inherent in these conversations. And operationalizing this can be as simple as holding a pre-engagement meeting to introduce people who are participating, to processes and timelines. Third, sustained engagement. We should create opportunities for repeated and iterative youth engagement. We can do this through multiple consultations or even through the creation of youth advisory boards and climate councils. And fourth, we should also involve youth in the implementation of green policies. Instead of just youth being policy designers, we should consider how these policies are linked to green jobs pathways, skill development, and long-term careers. So by incorporating these 4 pillars— vision, capacity building, sustained involvement, and green jobs— we can create governance models that work in a variety of urban contexts.
Thank you so much, Sushmita. To Alison, how can youth-led green public spaces act as both a climate buffer and a protective shield for marginalized youth?

Thank you for the question. Youth-led green spaces reclaim the right to the city and to the environment. They promote social environmental justice and reduce the incidence of diseases and climate-related disasters, especially for marginalized populations. By acting as agents of local climate adaptation, we as young people develop the infrastructure of our communities, care for the collective well-being, and create leisure spaces in historically neglected areas. At the same time, we create safe spaces for gathering and learning, strengthening the sense of community, building identities, and steering young people away from drugs and crime. These spaces protect marginalized youth while advancing climate justice and social inclusion. Those who are made— who are most marginalized and made vulnerable are creating solutions to overcome hardships within our own communities because life cannot wait. If floods arrive before adaptations and houses collapse before funding, that's why marginalized youth are leading solutions even without resources to survive, to seek for dignity, to build a better world. Therefore, youth-led green spaces reaffirm that the right to the city is not only about having a place to sleep, It's about having dignified housing, clean water and power, decent work that does not kill through exhaustion, and safe spaces for women, immigrants, LGBTQI people, and people from diverse backgrounds. That's why to speak about sustainable cities is also to speak about a little of every other SDG. Thank you.

Yes, a really great point made by my co-panelists. I think that participation is certainly a key issue that needs to be addressed, but I also diagnose the problem at the level of power sharing. To provide one example, I think I would point to the French deliberative climate assemblies. Ordinary residents were selected to participate. They were provided with and partnered with experts to collaborate to get the information that they needed to participate in those deliberations. They were well compensated for their time and expenses, and they were supported through a structured deliberation process to come up with their own ideas, and ultimately were given real legitimating power to make important decisions with decision makers like parliamentarians. And I think it showed a very compelling example of how everyday people, including young people, could make meaningful contributions to governance. And I think that when we want to move from symbolic representation to substantive representation, I think what that means is that young people become partners and co-collaborators in the urban future. And I think that means that young people participate as that permanent partners in governance. And so it's important for young people to have defined roles in things like climate commissions and transport agencies. But I also think we must be able to include the true diversity of youth, not just the most polished of youth, not just the most experienced of youth, but all types of youth from all different backgrounds. We must include students, workers, migrants, disabled youth, young parents, and those from underserved neighborhoods to truly participate in this urban future. And I think that allows young people to identify problems, set their own priorities, design solutions with others, especially when institutions are able to play a convening role and really facilitate that level of dialogue, both amongst youth and amongst larger communities. Thank you.

Also, traditional knowledge within each community is unique because it builds solutions rooted in local realities. What youth have been doing is not importing ideas from other countries, but integrating innovation with existing community practices. In this context, innovation does not mean breaking with the past, but recognizing that the answer has always been in the territory. Traditional communities present solutions that should be studied, expanded, and supported. In Brazil, for example, Afro-Brazilian religions such as Candomblé and Jurema Sagrados Sagrada play a significant role. This community develops resilience, cultivates environmental care practices, and provides safe spaces for LGBTQI people. In these religions, the sacred is found in nature. Oxum is the river, Iemanjá is the sea, Oiá is the wind. For these Tejero youth, to worship is to care, because we understand that we too are the nature. It is from this perspective that youth initiatives engage with these forms of knowledge. This is the case of my project, Quilombo Cidadão, in Recife, which connects innovation with Afrocentric education to develop identity, sense of community among Black and peripheral youth. Its goal is to contribute to leadership development and strengthening of their community, as well as to confront racism and violence. In this way, public facilities are transformed into spaces for sport talent development, and leadership formation, demonstrating how local practices can be integrated into youth-led urban solutions. Thank you.
